passage:
Arnab's salary was late again, and Vidya's parents were arriving on Sunday for their first visit to the one-room flat. Arnab had already booked a caterer and bought new curtains and a dinner set on the credit card, telling himself, 'They can't think we're struggling.' On Saturday night the card was declined at the sweet shop. He stood at the counter, face hot.
At home Vidya found the bills on the table. 'Arnab, Baba grew up eating khichuri on a mat. He's coming to see us, not our curtains.' They cancelled the caterer. On Sunday Vidya made khichuri and begun bhaja, and Arnab served it on their old plates. Her father asked for seconds and told stories till midnight.

qa.q: What did Vidya make on Sunday?
qa.a: Khichuri and begun bhaja.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when the card was declined?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and panicked, his face hot, afraid of looking poor in front of Vidya's parents.

qa.q: What went wrong with Arnab's plan, and what helped fix it?
qa.a: He spent beyond what they had to impress the guests; an honest talk with Vidya and a simple home-cooked meal eased the strain.

qa.q: How might Vidya's father have seen the simple Sunday dinner?
qa.a: He seemed truly happy and at home, asking for seconds and telling stories, showing the warmth mattered more than the display.

grounding: Shows a host who spends beyond his means out of fear of looking poor, and discovers that a warm, simple welcome is still real hospitality.

passage:
Tanuja had been planning the reunion lunch in her small Dadar flat for a month. Her old school friends were managers and designers now; she was still a junior clerk. So she bought paneer, prawns, fancy chocolates and a new tablecloth, borrowing from her sister to cover it. On the morning of the lunch she stood in the kitchen counting what was left for the month, and her stomach knotted.
Ritu arrived early and found her staring at the prawns. 'Tanu, what's wrong?' Out it all came. Ritu hugged her. 'We came for you and your aai's poha, silly. Remember school tiffins?'
That afternoon everyone laughed over poha and prawns alike, and nobody mentioned the tablecloth.

qa.q: What was Tanuja's job?
qa.a: A junior clerk.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling as she counted what was left for the month?
qa.a: She felt anxious and ashamed, worried about the money she had borrowed and spent so as not to look poorer than her friends.

qa.q: What could Tanuja keep in mind for the next get-together?
qa.a: That a warm, simple meal like her aai's poha is real hospitality; her friends came to see her, not an expensive spread.

qa.q: How did Ritu see Tanuja's worry?
qa.a: Ritu saw it with affection, reminding Tanuja that the friends came for her and for simple poha, not for show.

grounding: Illustrates a host who borrows and overspends to impress visitors out of fear of looking poor, and learns from a friend that a simple, warm welcome is enough.

passage:
When Nadia and three old classmates flew into Seoul, Soo-ah booked the rooftop restaurant everyone posted photos of. She paid for all five dinners on her card before anyone could reach for a wallet.

She couldn't look poor. Not in front of the girls who remembered her family's tiny noodle stall.

At two in the morning she lay awake, doing sums on her phone. Rent was due in nine days.

On the last evening Nadia said, "Can we just stay in tonight? I want what your mum used to make us after school."

So Soo-ah made tteokbokki in her small kitchen, in her one good pot. They sat on the floor in socks until midnight, laughing about old teachers.

At the airport Nadia hugged her. "Last night was the best part of the whole trip."

qa.q: How many days until Soo-ah's rent was due?
qa.a: Rent was due in nine days.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling as she lay awake at two in the morning?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt anxious and afraid about the rent after overspending so she wouldn't look poor.

qa.q: What choice could Soo-ah make the next time she hosts?
qa.a: Choose a simple welcome at home, like the tteokbokki night, and if the spending has left her worried, talk it through with someone she trusts.

qa.q: How does Nadia experience the two kinds of evening?
qa.a: Nadia enjoyed the rooftop, but found the simple night in socks on the floor the best part of the trip.

grounding: Shows a host who overspends to avoid looking poor, anxious afterwards, and discovering that a warm, simple welcome is the real hospitality.

passage:
It was Gopika's turn to bring Friday snacks for the eleven staff at the bank branch, and last month Mrs Iyer had brought catered samosas and imported chocolates.

So Gopika ordered a full spread from the costly sweet shop, then a cake, then paneer rolls. She told herself it didn't matter. It was nearly a quarter of what she sent home each month.

At the staff table she watched faces while they ate, smiling too hard.

Mohit, the senior cashier, came over with his plate. "You didn't have to do all this."

"Everyone brings nice things."

"Everyone still remembers the poha you brought at Diwali," he said. "We asked Iyer ma'am for the recipe, and she said, ask Gopika."

Gopika laughed, and something in her chest loosened. Next month, she decided, it would be poha.

qa.q: How many staff are at the bank branch?
qa.a: There are eleven staff at the bank branch.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling as she watched faces at the staff table?
qa.a: Gopika felt anxious and eager to impress, smiling too hard and afraid of looking less generous than Mrs Iyer.

qa.q: What choice does Gopika make, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: She decides to bring poha next month; a simple, warm offering is still real hospitality without the strain.

qa.q: How does Mohit see Gopika's spread?
qa.a: Mohit thinks she didn't need to do so much; he and the others already value the simple poha she once brought.

grounding: Shows a young host spending beyond her means out of fear of judgement, and realising a simple, warm offering is still real hospitality.

passage:
Dear Francis,

You asked how Diwali went with Sameer's whole family visiting. Honestly? It looked perfect. New dinner set, four kinds of sweets, a caterer for the second night. Sameer's Bua said, "Such a grand welcome!" and I glowed.

What I didn't tell anyone: most of it went on my card. I kept thinking, if it's simple, they'll say we're struggling, that his wife can't manage.

Now the bill has come, and my stomach drops every time I see the envelope.

The funny thing? The moment everyone loved most was the second morning, when Sameer's Dadi and I sat on the balcony with plain chai and she told me stories about his childhood.

I've decided to tell Sameer everything tonight, look at it together, and talk to someone at the bank about it.

Next time, chai on the balcony.

Parul

qa.q: What did Sameer's Bua say about the welcome?
qa.a: Sameer's Bua said, "Such a grand welcome!"

qa.q: How does Parul feel when she sees the bill envelope?
qa.a: Parul feels anxious and afraid; her stomach drops, after spending so as not to look like she couldn't manage.

qa.q: What choice has Parul made about the bill?
qa.a: To tell Sameer everything, look at it together, and speak with someone at the bank, instead of hiding it.

qa.q: What did the balcony morning seem to mean to Sameer's Dadi?
qa.a: Dadi seemed to enjoy simply sitting with Parul over plain chai and sharing stories, which needed no expense.

grounding: Shows a young host who overspends on a grand welcome out of fear of judgement, and realises the simplest moment was the real hospitality.

passage:
Mohit, you asked why I stopped doing big dinners, so here's the real story, from me, Vandana. Last year my husband's relatives came from Nagpur for a week. I wanted everything perfect. I didn't want his aunt saying we live small. So I ordered from the expensive caterer, bought new curtains, took them to a fancy restaurant twice. I put it all on the credit card. I smiled the whole week. Inside I was sick with worry. After they left, the bill came, and I cried in the bathroom. It took us months to sort it out with the bank.
And do you know what his aunt remembered? Not the curtains. She said, "Your aloo parathas on the last morning, with that green chutney. Just like my mother's." That was the cheapest meal of the week. Now I cook simple food, set the table nicely and sit down with my guests. Nobody has complained.

qa.q: What meal did the aunt remember?
qa.a: The aloo parathas on the last morning, with the green chutney.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel during the week of the visit?
qa.a: Vandana felt anxious and afraid of being judged, smiling outside but sick with worry inside.

qa.q: What did Vandana change, and why is it still real hospitality?
qa.a: Vandana now cooks simple food, sets the table nicely and sits with the guests; the warmth and time spent together are what guests actually remember.

qa.q: How might the aunt have felt about the visit?
qa.a: The aunt seemed warmly touched by the simple parathas, which reminded her of her mother, more than impressed by the expensive things.

grounding: It illustrates a host who spends beyond her means to avoid looking poor, and learns a warm simple welcome is real hospitality.
